Hey!
I'm a full-stack developer, student, and builder at the intersection of AI and space tech. I specialize in turning complex data into intuitive, high-impact software. Competing solo on the Flame in Freefall challenge, I’m leveraging NASA’s open datasets to model microgravity combustion and engineer a solution that advances spacecraft safety. Ready to build something extraordinary!
summary: AERO-PSI is an SI-powered research platform that connects NASA experimental data with aerosol modeling to explore how smoke behaves in microgravity. It combines gravity-dependent particle coagulation simulations, multi-angle optical scattering calculations, and automated experiment-gap finding in one interactive workspace. Users can investigate NASA smoke and combustion records, compare physical scenarios, visualize changing particle populations, and explore how those changes affect modeled light scattering. Integrated scientific intelligence explains concepts, interprets evidence and calculated results, ranks relevant investigations, and helps identify measurements needed to test a hypothesis. The platform distinguishes experimental observations from assumptions and simulations, keeping sources and scientific limitations visible. By bringing scattered records and complementary analysis tools together, AERO-PSI helps students and researchers move from exploring existing experiments to asking better scientific questions. Its goal is to make microgravity aerosol research more accessible and reproducible, supporting future investigations into smoke behavior and fire detection inside spacecraft and future habitats.
details:
AERO-PSI: Aerosol Evidence, Coagulation, Scattering, and Experiment Intelligence for Spacecraft Smoke Research

View Github Repository


AERO-PSI is an interactive scientific-computing platform for analyzing spacecraft-fire smoke as an evolving aerosol system. Its central idea is to connect three technical problems that are usually separated:

1. Aerosol evolution: How can a particle population change through Brownian coagulation, settling, removal, sources, growth, and transport assumptions?
2. Optical response: How does a particle-size distribution affect multi-angle light scattering?
3. Experimental evidence: Which NASA measurements support, constrain, or fail to validate a proposed physical explanation?

The project integrates deterministic aerosol physics, angular scattering calculations, NASA experiment records, and evidence-aware Scientific Intelligence into one workflow. The platform is designed for spacecraft fire-safety research, where smoke aerosols can affect crew health, visibility, filtration, and smoke-detection systems. In microgravity, smoke transport and particle evolution can differ substantially from terrestrial expectations because gravity-driven settling is reduced while diffusion, coagulation, ventilation, electrostatics, and sampling dynamics may remain important.

What does AERO-PSI do?

AERO-PSI provides a connected analysis environment with four major layers.

1. NASA Evidence Explorer

AERO-PSI organizes supplied NASA PSI materials into a searchable scientific archive. It brings together experimental tables, run workbooks, housekeeping records, reports, presentations, and investigation metadata from SAME-R / PSI-101, SAME / PSI-102, BASS, BASS-II, FLEX, ACME, SAFFIRE, and related fire-safety investigations.

  • Users inspect original source rows, columns, units, run conditions, material context, and related documents.
  • The platform calculates extrema, first-to-last changes, missing values, possible instrument sentinels, and operating-state transitions directly from selected records.

2. Aerosol Coagulation Model

AERO-PSI includes a physics-based sectional coagulation model for exploring how smoke-particle populations evolve. Users define an initial aerosol population, gas conditions, gravity level, particle density, sticking efficiency, residence time, sources, growth, and removal mechanisms.

  • The solver divides particles into logarithmic size sections and calculates collisions across the distribution.
  • It tracks particle number, surface area, volume, mass, equivalent volume-mean diameter, source/loss budgets, overflow, and volume conservation.
  • Users compare microgravity, terrestrial-gravity, and intermediate-gravity scenarios.
  • Numerical sensitivity checks compare different size-grid resolutions.

3. Multi-angle optical scattering model

The scattering model calculates how spherical smoke particles interact with light at multiple angles. Users select a particle-size distribution, wavelength, medium refractive index, particle refractive index, and viewing angles.

  • The model uses Mie theory, with Rayleigh theory available in the appropriate small-particle range.
  • It can use an assumed particle distribution or a distribution produced by the coagulation model.
  • Users can examine how particle size, concentration, refractive index, wavelength, and angle affect predicted scattering.
  • The module connects particle evolution with theoretical smoke-detector optical response.

4. Experiment gap finder and Scientific Intelligence

The gap finder turns a research question into an evidence and experiment-planning workflow. It ranks relevant NASA investigations, identifies available datasets and report passages, checks which measurements are present, and highlights the measurements or controls that would strengthen a future comparison.

  • It can identify relevant particle concentration, size distribution, flow, aging, temperature, pressure, gravity, wall-loss, and calibration information.
  • It distinguishes available evidence from information that still needs to be measured or confirmed.
  • Scientific Intelligence summarizes selected tables, interprets model outputs, explains scientific mechanisms, displays inline data plots, and supports follow-up questions.
  • Responses distinguish findings in the selected dataset, model calculations, possible explanations, and unresolved questions.
  • Source-specific SI findings provide direct citations to the relevant NASA datasets and documents.

What benefits does AERO-PSI have?

AERO-PSI makes complex spacecraft-smoke research easier to investigate by connecting NASA evidence, aerosol physics, optical modeling, and experiment planning in one platform.

  • Faster archive exploration: Users can search NASA investigations, inspect original rows and columns, and connect tables to reports and run context.
  • Particle-evolution analysis: The coagulation model shows how particle number, size distribution, surface area, volume, and mass may change under selected physical conditions.
  • Detector-research insight: Multi-angle scattering links particle properties to theoretical optical response.
  • Better experiment design: The gap finder identifies available evidence and the measurements needed to strengthen a proposed conclusion.
  • Traceable SI: Source-specific SI findings link back to the NASA datasets and documents used.
  • Accessible research: Interactive graphs, dark/light modes, larger text, high contrast, and reduced-motion support make the platform easier to use

What is the intended impact?

AERO-PSI aims to make spacecraft fire and smoke-aerosol research more understandable, traceable, and useful for future experiment design.

Smoke aerosols are important for crew safety, visibility, filtration, contamination control, and smoke detection. Historical spacecraft-fire records contain valuable evidence, but interpreting them requires connecting particle behavior, optical response, experimental conditions, and instrument limitations.

The intended impact is to help researchers, students, mission designers, and technical reviewers use NASA archive evidence more effectively when studying smoke behavior and designing future spacecraft-fire experiments

SoFIE microgravity flame imagery - credits to NASA

What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did you use?

  • Frontend - HTML, CSS, JavaScript: Built the interactive AERO-PSI interface, scientific dashboards, graph controls, source browser, SI workspace, accessibility settings, and dark/light themes.
  • Backend - Python and a structured JSON API: Handles scientific calculations, source analysis, evidence retrieval, data validation, browser-private investigation processing, and communication with the web interface.
  • Numerical computing - NumPy and SciPy: Supports numerical calculations, particle-distribution processing, scientific data analysis, and model diagnostics.
  • Optical calculations - miepython: Used for Mie-theory calculations of angular light scattering from spherical particle distributions.
  • Aerosol physics - Sectional Smoluchowski coagulation solver: Models particle collisions, size-distribution evolution, settling, sources, losses, conservation, and sensitivity across particle-size sections.
  • Scientific Intelligence - Google Vertex AI / Gemini: Powers evidence-aware scientific discussions, source-linked summaries, model interpretation, follow-up questions, and experiment-planning support.
  • Hosting - Google Cloud Run: Hosts the public AERO-PSI web platform and Python backend.
  • Data storage - Google Cloud Storage: Stores the verified scientific runtime archive used by the deployed platform.
  • Deployment - Cloud Build and Artifact Registry: Builds the application container and deploys versioned releases to Cloud Run.
  • Source control - Git and GitHub: Used to manage project versions, commits, development history, and the public project repository.
  • Development assistance - Codex: Used for AI-assisted software development, testing, interface implementation, and documentation drafting under team direction.
  • Scientific resources - NASA PSI archive: Includes NASA investigation tables, reports, workbooks, metadata, and supporting documents from spacecraft fire and smoke-aerosol research.
  • Mermaid - Diagrams
  • Canva - Pitch deck and DECODE101 banner

How is your project creative?

AERO-PSI is creative because it reimagines a historical research archive as an interactive scientific reasoning system.

Instead of presenting NASA datasets as files to browse, it turns them into an active investigation loop. A user can begin with a real measurement, ask what it may indicate, test a physical particle-evolution scenario, observe how that scenario changes predicted angular scattering, and then identify the exact missing measurements needed to evaluate the explanation.

  • Evidence becomes interactive: A NASA source row remains inspectable while its trend is plotted and discussed.
  • Models are connected: A coagulation-generated particle-size distribution can become an input to the multi-angle scattering calculation.
  • SI remains contextual: Scientific Intelligence stays attached to the selected NASA dataset, model result, or graph point instead of becoming a generic chatbot.
  • Uncertainty becomes useful: Missing information is transformed into a proposed measurement requirement instead of an empty result.
  • The user can move forward: AERO-PSI helps users progress from “What happened?” to “What could explain it?” to “What would we need to measure to test that explanation?”

Most tools either provide a graph without explaining its scientific limits or generate an explanation without showing where it came from. AERO-PSI makes the boundary between evidence, calculation, assumption, and uncertainty visible and interactive.

Use of Super Intelligence (SI)

Google Vertex AI

Google Vertex AI powers the platform’s Scientific Intelligence features. It helps users summarize selected evidence, interpret deterministic model outputs, explain scientific concepts, support follow-up questions, and identify possible measurement gaps. Source-specific findings provide direct citations to the relevant NASA datasets or documents

Codex

Codex was used as a supplementary AI-assisted development tool for selected coding tasks, debugging, testing, and documentation. Google Gemini was used for preliminary brainstorming, refining ideas, and reviewing aspects of the project. Both tools supported the development process, while the project's scientific methodology, architecture, and implementation were independently directed and developed.
